newsitem.title: GERMANY: Receiver denies pressure to keep Vulkan STN German.
newsitem.headline: Receiver denies pressure to keep Vulkan STN German.

text.p: The receiver in charge of liquidating Bremer Vulkan Verbund AG denied on Friday the government was blocking a foreign sale of the engineering group's defence electronics unit STN Atlas Elektronik.

Jobst Wellensiek referred to a report in Friday's Financial Times that the defence ministry had intervened against a bid for STN which British Aerospace was trying to mount with Daimler-Benz unit Dasa.
"The information that was published cannot be right. The sale is going completely to plan," Wellensiek told Reuters by telephone from Bremen.
He said that a bidding process, in which Rothschild merchant bank is acting as a consultant, was near completion and that 30 offers had been made for STN.
He said he hoped that a sale would be completed either this year or in early 1997. "We are interested in a full takeover," Wellensiek said.
The defence ministry in Bonn earlier this summer wrote to Wellensiek requesting STN stay under German control, because of its importance in torpedo, sonar and anti-mine production.
Wellensiek said he was aware of the defence ministry position, but said that he was not under any pressure to keep STN in German hands.
"I know the interests of the defence ministry, but I am not under pressure. They have no direct say in the sale," he said.

STN is the only profitable unit of Bremer Vulkan, which collapsed earlier this year after a scandal involving the alleged misuse of hundreds of millions of marks in state aid cleared by the European Union for use in eastern Germany.
Losses of 1.5 billion marks ($991.5 million) last year wiped out parent Bremer Vulkan's equity capital, but STN posted an operating profit of 32.5 million marks on sales of 1.45 billion marks.

STN could fetch a price of 400 to 800 million marks, but a German-only solution could hit the sale price and jeopardise attempts to refund money to Bremer Vulkan's creditors, sources close to the sale said.
German defence ministry officials and British Aerospace were not immediately available for comment, but Wellensiek said that a BAe-Dasa joint bid was among those he was reviewing.
